description: We are GeoSeekers, solving the "Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars" challenge for NASA Space Apps Cairo.
summary:
TerraX identifies and characterizes places on Earth that resemble the Moon or Mars. It's an interactive map: click any place, or draw a box of up to 220 km to scan, and TerraX scores each 22 km square. It uses open data: NASA GIBS imagery, ASTER terrain, MODIS surface temperature and summer vegetation, NASA POWER climate, and Macrostrat geology. A machine-learning model returns a verdict, Moon analog, Mars analog, both, or neither, with a confidence level, the reasons behind it, a comparison with known analog sites, and a colour comparison with NASA PDS lab measurements of real Apollo soil and Martian samples.

The model learned from 110 places, each cited to a documented source: Apollo astronaut training sites, the ESA Catalogue of Planetary Analogues, and NASA and USGS field tests. It classifies places it has never seen with about 89% accuracy.

Mission teams test rovers, landing systems and astronauts at analog sites before they fly, but those sites were found one at a time and aren't fully characterized. TerraX turns that expertise into a global screening tool for new test sites.
details:
What it does and how it works

TerraX finds places on Earth that resemble the Moon or Mars, and explains why.

On the interactive world map, a user clicks a place or draws a box of up to 2° × 2° (about 220 km, 100 squares) to scan. For each 22 × 22 km square, TerraX:

  1. Gathers open data for 48 × 48 pixels of about 460 m:
    • surface colour (NASA Blue Marble);
    • terrain relief (ASTER, via NASA GIBS);
    • daytime ground temperature in January and July (MODIS);
    • summer vegetation (MODIS NDVI);
    • long-term climate (NASA POWER);
    • rock type (Macrostrat geologic maps).
  2. Turns the data into 15 measurements per pixel, such as colour, terrain roughness, humidity, temperature swing, summer greenness and rock type. GIBS serves temperature and vegetation as coloured map images, so TerraX converts each colour back into a physical value (kelvin, NDVI) using NASA's published colour keys.
    • a confidence level (high, medium or low);
    • the three measurements that pushed the answer most;
    • a conditions table comparing the place with typical documented Moon and Mars analogs;
    • the most similar known analog;
    • a colour comparison with NASA PDS lab spectra of returned Apollo lunar soil, JSC Mars-1 dust simulant and Martian meteorites;
    • a caution for cases the model is known to struggle with.

The model learned from 110 places: 26 Moon analogs, 45 Mars analogs and 39 ordinary places. Every analog is cited: Apollo astronaut training sites (USGS Open-File Report 2005-1190), the ESA/Open University Catalogue of Planetary Analogues, and NASA, JPL, USGS, ESA and peer-reviewed sources. The ordinary places include 12 dry "hard negatives", such as steppe and dryland farms, so dryness alone isn't enough to count as an analog. Tested on places it never saw during training, it is correct 89% of the time.

Benefits

  • Speed: a whole region is screened in under a minute instead of one field trip at a time.
  • Explainability: every answer comes with measurable reasons, such as "summer greenness 0.08" or "seasonal ground-temperature swing 44 K".
  • Honesty: confidence levels, cautions and documented limitations show users when to trust a result.
  • Open and accessible: only free, open data, no API keys, and it runs on an ordinary laptop.

Intended impact

Mission teams test rovers, landing systems and astronauts at analog sites before they fly, but those sites were identified one by one and aren't fully characterized. TerraX turns that expertise into a global first-pass screening tool:

  • Mission planners can find new, closer or more accessible test sites for Artemis and future Mars missions.
  • Scientists get a data-based shortlist before committing to fieldwork.
  • Students and the public can explore why a landscape looks like another world.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML, CSS.
  • Machine learning and data: LightGBM, scikit-learn, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow, requests, joblib, matplotlib.
  • Development: Jupyter Notebook, VS Code, Git and GitHub.
  • Website: Flask (server and API) and Leaflet (interactive map), with Esri World Imagery, NASA Blue Marble and OpenStreetMap base maps, and OpenStreetMap Nominatim for place search.
  • Data services: NASA GIBS (WMS), NASA POWER API, NASA PDS Geosciences Node (RELAB), Macrostrat API.
  • Data sources: the ESA Catalogue of Planetary Analogues, the USGS Apollo training record, NASA, JPL, USGS and peer-reviewed analog studies, and Wikidata (site coordinates).
  • Hardware: a standard Windows laptop. No GPU or paid cloud services.

What makes it creative

  • Recovering science from map images: NASA's coloured visualization layers are converted back into physical measurements with the published colour keys, which makes a large catalogue of NASA data usable without downloading huge raw files.
  • Comparison with real Moon and Mars samples: every result is compared with lab spectra of returned Apollo soil and Martian meteorites. We also tested these spectra as model inputs. They didn't improve accuracy, which revealed a real finding: Earth's Moon analogs, such as red cinder fields, are redder than actual lunar soil.
  • A "Both" verdict: some places resemble both worlds (the Catalogue describes Atacama, Iceland and Meteor Crater that way), so TerraX doesn't force one answer.
  • Efficient area scanning: each NASA image layer is downloaded once per block and cut into squares, and climate data is shared between neighbouring squares, so a 100-square scan takes under a minute, with a progress bar.
  • Explanations a non-expert can read: per-place reasons and a comparison with real analog sites.

Factors the team considered

  • Data validity: every training label is backed by a citable source. Sites we couldn't document were removed (Haleakala, Mauna Kea). Sites whose sources didn't support their label were relabelled (Pisgah and the Ka'u Desert, from Moon to Mars).
  • Fair testing: pixels from one place are near-copies, so testing holds out whole regions (places within 150 km stay together) to avoid inflated scores.
    • 460 m resolution;
    • cold tundra resembles the polar Mars analogs, so the website shows a caution;
    • there's no feature for cities;
    • a score means "looks similar in these data", not a scientific certification.
  • Responsible use of free services: scans are capped at 100 squares, downloads run 12 at a time, and everything is cached so data is downloaded only once.
  • Reproducibility: the whole pipeline is in one documented notebook, with a requirements file of tested version ranges and a README that starts with the website.
